subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Bottleneck Theory
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Bottleneck Theory usable.

hook.text: Flash two signals and ask for two responses. Even trained subjects can't process both at once.

buildup.text: Welford and Pashler found a central bottleneck: only one decision can occupy the processor at a time.

discovery.text: Perception and motor responses can overlap, but the decision stage is strictly single-threaded.

twist.text: This bottleneck persists even after years of practice. It appears hardwired, not trainable.

climax.text: It explains why texting and driving is dangerous: both require the same single decision channel.

punchline.text: Your brain can sense two things but decide only one.

quiz.question: What does bottleneck theory say is single-threaded?

details.summary: Bottleneck theories propose that information processing narrows at a specific stage, forcing serial handling of competing inputs. Whether the bottleneck occurs early during perception or late during response selection remains debated, but the core insight is that parallel processing has hard limits.
details.whyItMatters: Bottleneck theory explains why dual-task performance suffers. It underpins interface design principles that avoid overwhelming users with simultaneous demands.
takeaways: A processing bottleneck forces serial handling at some stage
Early versus late bottleneck placement is still debated
The psychological refractory period demonstrates the bottleneck

faq.question: What is the psychological refractory period?
faq.answer: When two tasks requiring responses are presented in rapid succession, the second response is always delayed. This delay, the psychological refractory period, provides evidence for a central bottleneck that can only handle one response selection at a time.

faq.question: Can the bottleneck be bypassed with practice?
faq.answer: Extensive practice can reduce bottleneck effects by automating one or both tasks. Highly practiced tasks require fewer central resources. However, truly novel tasks still create a bottleneck, suggesting the limit is structural rather than entirely trainable.
